title: Al-A'la: the Most High
hookLine: glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned (87:1–3)

lines: THE LOWEST A BODY CAN GO.
cards: Watch Muslims pray, and there's one moment that stops people who've never seen it. The whole body goes down: knees, hands, and then forehead and nose on the floor. It's the lowest a human body can go while still awake.
And if you could hear what's being said, quietly, into the carpet, you'd hear a phrase about height. Not about being low. About the Most High.
That phrase comes straight from the opening line of the surah just before Al-Ghashiyah: Al-A'la, the Most High.

teach.b: Surah eighty-seven opens, in Pickthall's words: Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High. The Arabic is sabbih: glorify, declare perfect.

It's the root of subhanallah, glory be to God, a phrase this path met around day one hundred fourteen, counted thirty-three times on the fingers. And al-a'la, the Most High, from a root for height, being above.
Then the surah says who this is: the one who created, then proportioned; who measured, then guided. Everything made, then balanced, then given a direction. Now the link to prayer.
A hadith in Abu Dawud reports that when an earlier verse came, glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: put it in your bowing.
And when this verse came, glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, he said: put it in your prostration. So in the bowing, Muslims say subhana rabbiyal 'azim, glory to my Lord, the Magnificent.
With the forehead on the ground, subhana rabbiyal a'la, glory to my Lord, the Most High. Usually three times, or more.

teach.h: THE LOWEST PLACE, AND THE NEAREST.
teach.b: At the exact moment the body is lowest, the words are about height. It isn't humiliation.
It's perspective, like lying on your back under the night sky and suddenly knowing your size. Another hadith, in Muslim's collection, says the servant is closest to his Lord while in prostration.
The lowest place, and the nearest.

how: In every prostration of the prayer, Muslims say subhana rabbiyal a'la, glory to my Lord the Most High, usually three times, and in every bowing subhana rabbiyal 'azim; Al-A'la itself is often recited in the Friday, Eid and witr prayers.

o: the Most High, name of Surah eighty-seven
the bowing, said with hands on the knees
the night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: glory to my Lord, the Magnificent
glory to my Lord, the Most High

s: subhana rabbiyal a'la is said while bowing
it's said in prostration; the bowing has glory to my Lord, the Magnificent.
a hadith says the servant is closest to God in prostration
reported in Muslim's collection: the lowest place, and the nearest.
sabbih shares a root with subhanallah
s-b-h: to glorify, to declare perfect.

games.q: the verse 'glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High' is revealed. where does the Prophet say to put it?
o: at the end of the Qur'an
games.why: put it in your prostration (Abu Dawud). the words about height are said with the forehead on the floor.

practice: Let your body get a little lower than usual: sit on the floor if you can, or lower your head and let your shoulders drop, and feel the ground holding you while you think of the biggest thing you know, the sky, the ocean, the number of stars.
If you pray, you can say quietly, three times: subhana rabbiyal a'la. If not, just rest in the feeling of your size.

wordCard.voice: Al-A'la. The Most High, the name of Surah eighty-seven, and the words Muslims say with their foreheads on the ground. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "glory to my Lord, the Most High," said in each prostration of the prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: glory to the most high. The good kind of small, the night-sky kind. That's day two hundred one.

sources.q: Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High
